                    ### Question
                    A 70-year-old man presented to a medical clinic for a routine follow-up. He has had hypertension for 20 years and is currently on multiple anti-hypertensive medications. The blood pressure is 150/100 mm Hg. The remainder of the examinations were within normal limits. Echocardiography showed some changes in the left ventricle. What is the most likely reason for the change?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Disordered growth of the cardiac cells
opb. Replacement of cardiac cells into stronger red fiber skeletal cells
opc. Decrease in cardiac cell size
opd. Increase in cardiac cell size
ope. Increase in number of normal cardiac cells

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
Chronic hypertension leads to increased workload on the heart, resulting in left ventricular hypertrophy. This can cause changes in the left ventricle seen on echocardiography, possibly indicating an increase in cardiac cell size due to remodeling of the heart muscle. The evidence paths support the relationship between left ventricular structure, genes, and heme oxygenase-1 interacting with heart cells, which can contribute to the observed changes. Therefore, the most likely reason for the change in the left ventricle is an increase in cardiac cell size.
